prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: I keep a single-achievement B021 prize for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange did not change my scientific reasons: incretin physiology (Holst), proglucagon processing and receptor biology (Drucker) and the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide (Mojsov) form one continuous chain that led to drugs with large, independent outcome trials across glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal disease. The mechanism is settled and the interpretation has been stable for decades, so recognition is mature. The identical opening ranks are not my argument, and the chair is right to ask whether the configuration survives its stated weaknesses. After testing it against the alternatives, I find that it does, because every alternative has a credit problem that is at least as serious as the GLP-1 one and a weaker maturity or remit fit. I would word the citation around physiology and the active peptide and say openly that this is a choice about what the prize rewards, not a finding that development is unimportant. I prefer a one-part prize to a two-part prize because the three-person cap would force GLP-1 down to two names to make room for any second part, and I see no second part that four members would support without a comparable attribution objection.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and unresolved by the record we were given: priority for the active truncated peptide between Mojsov and the Habener group, with Habener outside the credited names. I cannot settle it from the supplied evidence, and several members, myself included, say their account is partly recalled. The second reservation is that leaving out Lotte Bjerre Knudsen means the prize rewards the discovery and not the drug that reached patients, so a reader could call the citation incomplete. Neither is a scientific objection to the mechanism, but together they mean the configuration is defensible and not unassailable. If four members conclude the Mojsov claim cannot be stated without a priority judgement, the citation would have to be reworded to avoid it, or the committee would have to accept that the active-peptide step is credited only in part.

responses.point: The chair calls the Knudsen question the sharpest challenge to B021 and says that if translation must be recognised, the choice is between Knudsen and Mojsov, with a lean towards keeping Mojsov. He asks whether four members accept a physiology-centred citation.
responses.response: I accept the physiology-centred citation and I would vote for it. I also agree with you that Knudsen's exclusion should not be treated as obvious: it is a stated policy line, and the citation should say what it rewards. I would keep Mojsov over Knudsen for the reason you give, since the active peptide is what everything downstream is built on, and because swapping Mojsov for Knudsen would turn a discovery prize into a development prize while leaving the priority dispute just as open. On your question about a second part, I do not see one yet: B032 would need GLP-1 trimmed to two names, and I would not weaken the strongest part to carry a weaker one.

responses.point: She would keep the three physiology names and argues that any replacement by Knudsen needs an explicit rationale, most plausibly where priority is most disputed. She also keeps B032 (Feldmann and Maini) as an alternative with a clean pair and over twenty-five years of confirmation.
responses.response: Your test is the right one: displacing a laureate needs a stated ground, and the only ground on the table is the Mojsov priority dispute, which a missing record does not settle in either direction. Absence of evidence is not evidence against her claim, so I would not remove her on that basis. On B032, I accept that the attribution is cleaner than almost anything else and that maturity is a strength, and I respect that you disclosed your field familiarity. I still weigh it below B033 and B044 because it validates a cytokine target through antibody engineering and trials, with upstream TNF work by Old, Cerami and Beutler outside the credits. I now rate it a sounder fallback than I did in round 1, but I would not use it as a second part, since that would cost GLP-1 a laureate.

responses.point: Linnarsson keeps CAR-T second with June and Sadelain only, calls it arguably a more novel therapeutic modality than GLP-1, and criticised my round-1 optogenetics trio (Boyden, Deisseroth, Hegemann) for dropping the channelrhodopsin discoverers.
responses.response: Your criticism of my optogenetics trio is correct and I am changing it. Dropping Nagel and Bamberg in favour of the demonstrators makes a substantive claim about what the prize rewards, and I cannot defend that claim. If B044 is pursued I now prefer Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel, with the unresolved exclusion of Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenbock stated openly. I note this is the same split that Perlmann, Sandberg and Svenningsson proposed in round 1. On CAR-T, I agree that June and Sadelain is the right CAR-specific pair, but I do not accept that its novelty puts it ahead of GLP-1 this year. Eshhar originated the chimeric receptor and is outside the credits, which a pair does not fix, and Wahren-Herlenius's points on long-term safety and activity beyond B-cell malignancy are real maturity questions that the GLP-1 record does not raise.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that B052 (UPR, Walter and Mori) is the better scientific case than B042 because it is a general principle of intracellular signalling, and says clean attribution does not outweigh the size of the GLP-1 effect, so she would not build a two-part prize around either.
responses.response: I agree with your last point and with part of the first. The UPR is a general principle, and Walter and Mori is as clean a pair as the list offers. I also take your point that I treated its translation as too indirect, which understates how much it explains about secretory-cell stress and disease. But general scientific importance is not the only criterion, and the will asks for greatest benefit to humankind. Here the GLP-1 effect on patients is far larger and is shown by trials. I also agree that B042 is a drug story for one disease with the SMN gene discovery uncredited, and I would still treat it as a later candidate. So I would not move either into a configuration this year, though I would keep B052 in view for a later year.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks B033 second but not as a clean attribution, calls optogenetics a methods prize with contested allocation, and says B033 is a strong second part only if the committee accepts a prize that omits Eshhar.
responses.response: I agree with your caution on both. A methods prize with a contested allocation is a harder fit than a mechanism or therapy, and I now think that is a real reason to keep B044 as an alternative and not a second part, which is firmer than my round-1 wording. On B033, your condition is the correct way to put it: it works as a second part only if the committee accepts omitting Eshhar. I do not accept that, and at four votes to carry it I doubt the committee would either. I also note your Knudsen position: you called her the natural fourth name, and I agree she is, but the three-person cap and the physiology-versus-development line decide it for me.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide can be stated without a ruling against Habener, which I cannot settle from the supplied record.
Whether four members accept a citation that openly leaves development, and therefore Knudsen, out of the prize.
If a second achievement were pursued, whether B033 or B044 could be credited fairly given Eshhar's absence and the six-name optogenetics claim.
Whether my reading of B032 as translation of upstream TNF biology is fair, as my account of that history is partly recalled.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level conflict for any shortlisted ballot. For transparency, I co-authored a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons, which does not relate to the shortlisted candidates. My motor-circuit field uses optogenetic tools, but I have no documented tie to any credited optogenetics candidate. I have no documented link to the GLP-1 candidates, and I note that GLP-1's central appetite action touches neuroscience without affecting my judgement.
